Class Scope

java.lang.Object
org.clafer.scope.Scope
All Implemented Interfaces:
Scopable
public class Scope extends Object implements Scopable

An immutable mapping from Clafers to their scope. Also contains the scope of integers for solving, like the bit-width in Alloy, but more flexible because the lowest and highest integers can be set independently and does not have to be a power of 2.

The scope is built through the constructor or ScopeBuilder, whichever is more convenient.

Example 1: 

Map<AstClafer, Integer> map = new HashMap<invalid input: '&gt'();
map.put(claferA, 3);
map.put(claferB, 2);
Scope scope = new Scope(map, 3, -16, 16, null, null, 10, (char) 0x20, (char) 0x7e);

Example 2: 

Scope scope = Scope.setScope(claferA, 3).setScope(claferB, 2).defaultScope(3).intLow(-16).intHigh(16).toScope();

Both examples construct the same scope.

What is scope? Because of the expressiveness of Clafer, reasoning is too difficult in general. The scope is a limitation of the solver so that reasoning is feasible.

Example 1: 

A : int
B : int
C : int
[A * A * A + B * B * B = C * C * C]

Example 2: 

A 2..*
B 2..*
C 2..*
[#A * #A * #A + #B * #B * #B = #C * #C * #C]

Both examples are attempting to prove/disprove Fermat's last theorem for k=3, although this easily generalizes for any k. Unfortunately this is too difficult, so the solver only attempts to prove/disprove upto a certain scope. In example 1, a scope of Scope.intLow(2).intHigh(16).toScope() would only attempt the proof for integers between 2 and 16. In example 2, a scope of Scope.defaultScope(16).toScope() would also only attempt the proof for integers between 2 and 16 (the example uses encodes integers using cardinality).
